## Intent
Hypothesis: manual loop unrolling over particles can amortize per-particle branch overhead and expose ILP on the AoS layout, narrowing the gap to auto-vectorized variants.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS layout offers 32 hot bytes (47%) to loop 1 — age+pos+seed+vel — and 28 hot bytes (41%) to loop 2 — color+pos — meaning over half of each 64 B cache-line fill is dead weight dragged through the line filler. No intermediate storage is allocated; the death verdict stays in registers, which is beneficial but does not relieve the line-filler tax. The approach unrolls loop 1 by four (visible in the four repeated blocks at stride 0x44 = 68 B), aiming to amortize loop overhead and overlap the branchy respawn across particles. With 53–59% dead bytes per line and a per-particle branch chain that cannot be hoisted, the unroll has little to amortize: the working set spills L1d at N≈481 and L2 at N≈7710, but the dead-byte fraction effectively halves cache capacity without changing the per-particle instruction mix.

## Cache saturation
The ns/p curve is strikingly flat across all regimes. At q=0.01, cost rises from 21.5 ns/p in L1d (N=320) to only 25.4 ns/p in DRAM (N=10M) — an 18% increase spanning the entire hierarchy, with no sharp knee at the L1d→L2 spill (N≈481), the L2→L3 spill (N≈7710), or the L3→DRAM spill (N≈246723). This flatness signals that the algo is not streaming-limited; backend stalls (59–65% of cycles) dominate whether the working set is L1d-resident or DRAM-resident. The dense grid resolves no transition because there is none to resolve — the dead-byte fraction degrades cache efficiency uniformly, and the per-particle branch chain sets a floor that cache residency cannot lift.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 2.6–3.2 GB/s against the 12.69 GB/s ceiling (20–25%) and against the 5.359 ns/p memory floor the algo runs at 4–6x floor — clearly not bandwidth-bound but backend-stall-bound (59–65%) with a rising branch_flush contribution (11.5% at q=0.01 to 15.3% at q=0.5). The algo matches the scalar baseline to within 0.96–1.0x at every N×q point: unrolling buys nothing. Versus the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt), it is 1.75–3.5x slower, with the gap narrowing as q rises (3.48x at q=0.01/N=160K versus 1.76x at q=0.5/N=370K) — the branchy respawn is the equalizer, hurting both algos but proportionally less for the winner which can still stream its vectorized integrate. Death rate scales cost linearly: 21.5 ns/p at q=0.01 to 33.1 ns/p at q=0.5, a 54% increase driven by branch_flush rising from 11.5% to 15%.

## Assembly
The codegen unrolls loop 1 by four (four repeated blocks at +0, +0x44, +0x88, +0xcc) using component-wise SSE: `vmovups` for 16 B pos loads, `vmulps`/`vaddps` for 3-component vector math, `vshufps`/`vinsertps` for lane shuffles — all intra-particle, never across particles, because AoS prevents cross-particle SIMD. The respawn path is deeply branchy: `vucomiss`+`jae`+`jne`+`jbe` chains with 15 `call` instructions to `spawn` and 50 cond-branches per loop-1 iteration. The render loop (loop 3) uses `cmovae` for select-based clamping but still performs byte-granular scatter: `movzx`+`add`+`cmp`+`cmovae`+`mov BYTE PTR` repeated ×17, capping any streaming potential. The 73 vector instructions are intra-particle only; the byte scatter and branch chains dominate cycle count, explaining why backend stalls hold at 59–65% regardless of cache regime.

## Verdict
Refuted — 0.96–1.0x of the scalar baseline at every N×q point (e.g., 0.971x at q=0.01/N=320, 0.99x at q=0.5/N=10M): manual unrolling buys nothing because the bottleneck is backend stalls (59–65%) and branch_flush (11.5–15.3%), not instruction throughput. The winner (autovec) is 1.75–3.5x faster (3.48x at q=0.01/N=160K, narrowing to 1.76x at q=0.5/N=370K), with the gap shrinking at high q where branchy respawn dominates both. Component-wise SSE on AoS cannot cross particle boundaries, and the 50 cond-branches/iter plus byte-granular render scatter prevent any streaming benefit from the unroll.
